title: [bug] syllabify() silently dropped unparseable word-initial clusters, so legal() accepted impossible words
description:
SELF-CAUGHT while inspecting round 5's concrete repair list, 2026-08-30. FIXED in tools/gz_redundancy.py with three regression tests in tools/test_gz_redundancy.py.

gz_redundancy.syllabify() splits an illegal onset cluster by handing the unparseable prefix to the PREVIOUS syllable's coda. Word-initially there is no previous syllable, and the prefix was silently discarded: syllabify('Cle') returned [('l','e','')], so legal('Cle') was True. Same for 'CCa', 'Cte', 'Csu'.

BLAST RADIUS. The round-5 repair pass chose forms by legality, so it was moving words into space that is empty precisely BECAUSE it is illegal — every one of the first ten repairs prefixed /ts/, /dZ/ or /J/. gz_redundancy's own nonword-vs-illegal breakdown also misclassified word-initial insertions as nonwords; the silent-error rate itself is unaffected (it tests lexicon membership, not legality). ez_structure and ez_semantics build forms by suffixation and never create word-initial clusters, so they are clean.

Fix: return None when the leading cluster cannot be parsed and there is no previous syllable to absorb it.

title: [bug] The minting pass's candidate ORDER was costing 17-95x in off-model robustness — round 1's central trade-off is an artifact
description:
FOUND BY: Codex review of round 5 (xhigh, 2026-08-30), confirmed and extended by tools/ez_frontier.py ez_order_sweep().

ez_mint.mint() walks its candidate list in a fixed order — shortest/simplest shapes first, then enumeration order — and takes the first unblocked candidate at each rank. That order is not a design decision; it is an artifact of how the pool was generated. A dense prefix scan packs the accepted words into one corner of the space, so they sit exactly at the design distance from each other with nothing left over for confusions the rule did not model.

Shuffling the candidate order WITHIN each length class (so short forms still go to frequent concepts) and holding everything else fixed — same word count, same edit-1 rule, same floor, same alphabet, same Zipf weights:

  floor 4:  off-model 3.96% -> 0.23% (median of 10);  two-error 8.5% -> 0.7%
  floor 5:  off-model 3.40% -> 0.06%;                 two-error 3.5% -> 0.1%
  floor 6:  off-model 2.86% -> 0.03%;                 two-error 2.5% -> 0.1%

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PAPER (paper/paper.md §4, the EZ paragraph). Round 1's headline cost — 'its advantage inverts past the design distance ... under a substitution-dominated channel the inherited lexicon wins' and the 'classical algebraic-versus-distributed trade' — does NOT survive. With a shuffled tie-break the minted lexicon's two-error rate is 0.1-0.7% against RZ's 7.2%. The trade-off round 1 reported as the textbook cost of engineering was a property of the enumeration, not of the code.

The 2.86% off-model figure currently in the paper must be replaced or narrowed to 'this dense-prefix baseline'.

GENERAL LESSON, worth a CLAUDE.md line: any greedy packing over an ordered candidate pool must randomise the arbitrary part of the order and report the distribution, or the result is a property of the enumeration.

title: Paper: make Interlingua the BASELINE, not a related-work entry — RZ is the demo instance, the contribution is priced deltas + method
description:
Edward 2026-08-30: 'whats the value of a paper for this over "ok so it's um, interlingua"?' — agreed the reframe, DEFERRED to this bead (not started).

## The problem
As 'we made a language' the paper is worth nothing: conlang-wan establishes RZ is ~80-85% Interlingua at the grammar level (literally shared forms), and as specced RZ is a fourth fork alongside Interlingua/Neolatino/LFN — the pathology romance-zonal-v0.md §7.5 warns against. Interlingua appears twice in 900 lines of paper/paper.md, as related work.

## The reframe
Interlingua is the BASELINE. The paper is: 'Interlingua was basically right; here are N priced improvements to a zonal auxlang, each with a mechanism and a number, and the instrument that tells you whether each paid.' RZ is the demo instance. The contribution is what Interlingua never produced:
1. The METHOD — ledger pricing in learner-hours, the mining gate, precommitted kill criterion (learning-budget.md, program.md).
2. PORTABLE ADD-ONS that work on any host incl. Interlingua itself — number/date/time modes w/ checksums, repair register (rz-repair-mode.md), error-absorption declarations D1-D7, chording over the phonology. Lane E toolkit entries.
3. Two RESULTS from the coding-theory lens — assignment policy dominates the register (humility, 22%→3.9%, §12) and repair-beats-minting (conlang-gpc, pending review): how to make ANY inherited lexicon error-robust with minimal transparency loss. Both apply directly to Interlingua's own lexicon.
4. The INSTRUMENT — cloze protocol with a stated objective function (ym3), the context Interslavic's 84% lacks.

## Why this is robust to the kill gate
If x6t says Interlingua reads as well as RZ, the add-ons apply to Interlingua (inherit its 27k-word dictionary, Wikipedia, community) and the paper is unchanged — arguably better; the S2 audience adopts methods, not languages.

## Scope
- Restructure paper/paper.md: abstract + §1 state the baseline framing; §9b/§10 give Interlingua a full baseline section (design method, what it got right, what it lacks — cite IALA 1951 primary source); each RZ delta becomes a priced entry against that baseline; §11 evaluation reads as 'does each delta pay'.
- Feeds conlang-wan (recommendation on record: ship as an Interlingua PROFILE — removes fork liability, matches the paper's actual contribution; human gate still Edward's).
- Blocks conlang-hf0 (publication) — publish under the reframe, not before.
- Caveat to keep in the text: without a measured number the paper is a design essay with a good simulation section; the humility and repair results are the only results-not-hypotheses in it.

title: Repair beats minting: the error-corrected lexicon you want is a repaired one, not a new one
description:
Round 5's headline, pending review. Size-matched at 518 words and scored off-model (the wider e~o/i~u graph neither lexicon may optimize against), a REPAIRED RZ dominates a MINTED EZ on every measured axis: 0.23% off-model one-error and a 1.7% two-error tail at 4.61 running segments, against the best minted lexicon's 2.86% / 2.5% at 6.00 segments — and it keeps 74% of running text on the donor's form (100% within one segment) where minting keeps 0%.

Proposed mechanism (stated in the doc, NOT yet isolated by an experiment): a minted lexicon is a maximally packed independent set, so every word sits exactly at the design distance and anything off-model lands outside it; an inherited lexicon wastes the space, and repair spends only the waste it has to. The isolating experiment would measure nearest-neighbour slack distribution for both at matched running length.

This reverses the direction rounds 1-4 were pointed in and needs the human gate before it goes in the paper as anything but a measured result.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: claude-conlang-ez
comments.text:
FALSIFIED, 2026-08-30, by the Codex review of round 5 (xhigh) and confirmed by tools/ez_frontier.py ez_order_sweep().

The claim rested on comparing repaired RZ against a MINTED lexicon built by a dense-prefix candidate scan. That scan was the whole of EZ's off-model weakness (bead conlang-4d8). With the candidate order shuffled within length classes, a floor-4 minted lexicon reaches 0.23% off-model and 0.7% two-error at 4.00 segments / 1.98 syllables — better than every repaired-RZ variant on robustness AND on both length measures.

WHAT REPLACES IT — an exchange rate, which is what the bead should have asked for:
  minted, floor 4 shuffled : 0.23% off-model, 0.7% two-error, 4.00 seg, 1.98 syl,  0% donor text
  repaired, greedy+stage2  : 0.42% off-model, 1.9% two-error, 4.61 seg, 2.13 syl, 67% donor text (98% within one segment)
  repaired, rarest-first   : 1.18% off-model, 1.6% two-error, 4.58 seg, 2.08 syl, 76% donor text (100% within one segment)
  RZ untouched             : 12.26% off-model, 7.2% two-error, 4.36 seg, 1.97 syl, 100%

Repair buys 67-76% of running text for ~0.6 extra segments and 2-5x the residual error rate. Neither endpoint dominates. That is the Pareto answer Edward asked for.

The proposed 'maximal packing' mechanism is also withdrawn: mint() does not produce a maximal independent set, it stops at N, and legal candidates remain at every floor.

Closing this as answered-by-refutation; the surviving statement lives in docs/design/ez-error-corrected-lexicon.md round 5.

title: RZ: eight paradigm repairs take silent errors from 10.73% to under 2% for 18% of running text
description:
Round 5 (docs/design/ez-error-corrected-lexicon.md, tools/ez_frontier.py) measured the repair frontier on RZ's actual lexicon. The curve is extremely concave: greedy repair by frequency-weighted damage takes the cross-lemma silent-error rate from 11.07% to 1.75% in TEN lemma repairs, leaving 88.2% of running text on the donor's exact form and 100% of it within one segment. 5 of 488 repair units carry half the entire silent-error mass, and the six largest carriers are all one- and two-segment function words.

This is a concrete, cheap, actionable change to RZ that does not need the EZ line to exist. It is a HUMAN GATE: it changes word forms a Romance reader currently gets for free, so Edward decides whether the transparency is spendable. What the tool can supply on request: the exact repair list with donor form, repaired form, edit distance, and damage removed.

Depends on the starboard/larboard coinage-screen work (conlang-ey6) and overlaps conlang-kww (nothing screens for dropped segments).

title: GZ particle space is 20/20 FULL and 'haan' is double-assigned: negation vs mode chunk-separator
description:
Found 2026-08-30 while pricing an Ithkuil steal (register particles) against GZ's particle budget. Audit script: scratchpad/particle_audit.py; reproduce by listing modes.py particles against gf-grammar.md section 3.

THE COLLISION:
- docs/spec/modes.md assigns h-a-n ('haan') = chunk separator / residue-100 escape.
- docs/design/gf-grammar.md section 3 assigns h-a-n ('haan') = NEGATION, and explicitly justifies the choice: 'deliberately long+nasal: a misheard negation inverts meaning, so it gets the most robust form'.
Both documents claim the cell independently and neither mentions the other.

Context disambiguation (inside a mode frame vs not) is the obvious defence, but it is exactly the kind of context-dependence GZ's unique-parse property (SPEC 5.2) exists to avoid, and negation is the single highest-stakes bit in any utterance — cf. conlang-1op, where RZ's unprotected polarity bit is already a P1.

THE BIGGER FINDING: the space is exactly full.
h + 5 vowels x 4 codas = 20 cells. Modes own 9, grammar owns 11 (incl. the collided haan) plus h-i-l reserved. Occupied: 20/20. Genuinely free cells: ZERO.

SPEC 5.2 anticipated exactly this: 'The particle namespace width is provisional in v0.1 - 20 lexical slots exist under the current template, but whether 20 suffices is established by conlang-jbw's enumeration BEFORE freeze, not assumed. If it overflows, widening the particle encoding (particle-only diphthongs or codas) is a real phonotactic change with script- and input-layer costs.'

The enumeration has now effectively happened and the answer is that 20 does NOT suffice: the inventory is full, with a collision, BEFORE adding any new mechanism. This is a freeze-gate blocker.

OPTIONS (need pricing):
1. Re-assign one of the two haan uses. Cheapest. The mode chunk-separator is rarer and lower-stakes than negation, but every free cell is taken, so this requires evicting something else or accepting a longer form.
2. Move a mode particle to a content word. Modes own 9 of 20 for a subsystem that is optional in casual speech.
3. Widen the particle namespace (SPEC 9 minor-version path: particle-only diphthongs or codas). Real phonotactic change; script and input layers must render the new shapes.
4. Push closed-class items to stressed content words, which gf-grammar's overflow policy already does for 'but/while/if'. Applies to particles too?

BLOCKS: any proposal needing new particles - including the Ithkuil register-particle steal (ithkuil-mining.md section 3, which needs up to 5) and the reserved-but-unbuilt phonetic/coordinate modes.

title: Round 5: the repair frontier — how much zonal transparency does error robustness cost?
description: Rounds 1-4 established two endpoints: RZ (inherited, transparent, 11.23% silent-error rate) and EZ (minted, opaque, ~0%). Edward's ask was the PARETO FRONTIER between them, not the endpoints. Round 5 walks it: start from the real RZ lexicon, repair the highest-damage words one paradigm at a time, and measure at every step both the silent-error rate and the share of running text a Romance reader still recognizes for free. Repair = minimal edit to the shared phonemic stem of a lemma, propagated to every inflected form, accepted only if all members are legal and clear of every other lemma. Controls: greedy-by-damage vs random vs rarest-first, to separate 'how many words you change' from 'which words you change'.

title: Round 4: syntax catches 84-100% of category errors and 0% of polarity errors
description:
tools/ez_sentence.py; docs/design/ez-error-corrected-lexicon.md 'Round 4'. Reviewed (Codex xhigh, 2026-08-30), corrections applied.

WHY: every earlier round measured isolated words and caveated 'no context modelling'. Round 3 then made that caveat load-bearing — it scored category confusions as cheap BECAUSE syntax should catch them, with the catch rate q unmeasured. This measures q by putting words in sentences (slot-template grammar, one word corrupted per sentence, 160k sentences per design, +-0.08 points at 2 sigma).

RESULT (damaging = a slip that survives syntax and changes stem or polarity):
  naive negator, markers by grammar   non-word 88.8% | syntax 8.3% | DAMAGING 2.87% | q(cat) 1.000 | q(pol) 0.000
  naive negator, markers blind        89.3% | 6.7% | 2.84% | q(cat) 0.844 | q(pol) 0.000
  hazard-aware negator                91.8% | 8.2% | 0.00% | 1.000 | -
  replacement portmanteau             92.3% | 7.7% | 0.00% | 1.000 | -
  no morphology at all               100.0% | 0.0% | 0.00% | - | -
All five: 2004 words, 334 stems, no duplicates, no illegal forms, asserted. The two marker maps select the SAME 334 stems, so the q difference is not stem-selection confounding (reviewer verified).

FINDING 1 — q is not one number but two: ~0.84-1.00 for category, exactly 0 for polarity. The round-3 assumption was right for categories and wrong to extend to polarity.

FINDING 2 — WHICH MARKER GOES ON WHICH CATEGORY is worth ~16 points of detection. The two naive rows differ ONLY in which vowel marks which part of speech. Categories that share a grammatical slot must not share a corner of form space; categories that never co-occur may sit as close as you like. Nothing in this project's channel design has ever consulted the grammar when assigning channel values.

FINDING 3 (narrowed by the review) — it is UNSPACED morphology, not morphology, that manufactures collisions. The hazard-aware and portmanteau designs keep full paradigms and still reach 0.00%. The tension is robustness vs LENGTH, as in round 1, not robustness vs having a morphology.

CORRECTIONS APPLIED: (a) BLOCKER — relabelling categories from exponents to glosses silently shifted round 3's within-paradigm frequency ranks and hence its cheap rates (naive 9.01->8.70, hazard 8.72->8.41) and its whole q-sensitivity table; all regenerated, and the tool now carries a comment saying the label convention is load-bearing. (b) q reported as 0.844 (exact enumeration 0.84405) rather than an overprecise sampled 0.848. (c) ambiguous-slot count corrected. (d) evidence markers added.

title: RZ + GN: the polarity marker is one segment and that is unsafe by construction
description:
Generalizes the EZ round-3 result (docs/design/ez-error-corrected-lexicon.md) to the shipping lines. Measured in tools/ez_semantics.py.

THE LAW: adding one segment IS one error. So a one-segment polarity marker is one slip from its own positive, for EVERY choice of segment. Swept all nine attested one-segment negators in the EZ phonology: identical 2.81% damaging rate, identical 1002-of-1002 same-slot pairs. Picking a 'distinctive' negation marker buys nothing, because the hazard is the insertion edge, not the segment identity.

WHERE THIS BITES THE EXISTING LINES:
- RZ negates with the clitic 'no', which round 1 measured as one confusable substitution from 'lo' (object clitic) — same preverbal slot, opposite truth value, both grammatical. Already filed as conlang-1op. This bead is the general form: it is not bad luck about n~l, it is that the most truth-critical distinction in the language is carried by the cheapest form in it.
- GN's check bit and humility rule are both about UNRELATED minimal pairs. Neither screens a word against its own negation, because those are related. Same blind spot.

THE FIX SHAPE, priced in EZ: give polarity two segments. Costs 10.3% word length, drives the damaging rate to zero, and improves two-error behaviour as a side effect. For RZ the additive version is the Jespersen answer already filed on conlang-1op (a second exponent in the high registers) since re-minting 'no' fails the first-contact gate.

THE PORTABLE RULE for the toolkit lane (conlang-wxm): frequency may set the LENGTH of a form, but never the DISTANCE between forms whose confusion changes truth. [D — design judgement from one measured system; many natural languages do mark negation with a single segment, which this predicts must be repaired by context or prosody rather than by form. TODO-verify against a typological survey before publication.]

title: NEXT: mint a STRUCTURED lexicon — does systematic form buy back the vocabulary-learning bill?
description:
The one axis ez_mint.py does not touch, and the one that decides whether EZ is worth anything: how much harder is an arbitrary vocabulary to learn? RZ gets its vocabulary ~free for a Romance reader; EZ pays full price. Nothing measured so far offsets that.

LIVE HYPOTHESIS [H — untested]: words built by rule are easier to memorize than arbitrary strings, and an error-correcting lexicon IS a rule-built lexicon. If the effect is large, part of the vocabulary bill comes back — and that is the actual Pareto-frontier question Edward asked for, rather than the form-axis one which turned out to have no trade-off in it.

The current minting pass optimizes DISTANCE ALONE and ignores structure entirely: no semantic fields sharing shape, no systematic derivation, no harmony or template constraints. So the measured EZ is the WORST case for learnability and still wins on form.

BUILD: mint a structured variant — semantic-field shape families, regular derivation, a template or harmony invariant — and measure what structure costs on the robustness axis. Early expectation is 'almost nothing', because the sound space has room (full strictness already costs ~0.05 syllables/word).

MEASURING THE LEARNABILITY SIDE: human testing is deferred by standing directive, so this needs a defensible computational proxy. Candidates: phonotactic predictability, morphological reuse (how many stems cover N concepts), and syllable-inventory load (already instrumented — min-6 EZ needs 134 distinct syllables vs RZ's 304). State the proxy's limits explicitly; do not let a proxy become a claim.

comments.author: claude-conlang-ec
comments.text:
DONE 2026-08-29 — built as tools/ez_structure.py; results in docs/design/ez-error-corrected-lexicon.md (Round 2 section).

LEARNABILITY MEASURE: description length. When a word is assigned, count how many forms were still legal at that moment; a free choice among K costs the learner log2(K) bits, a rule-determined form costs zero. Same quantity across variants, so the comparison is fair. NOT a claim about learner-hours [H].

RESULT (2000 concepts, min 4 segments, robustness rule fixed):
  arbitrary (round 1)   1-err 0.0% | 2-err 11.0% | 1.36 syl | 17.1 bits/word
  semantic fields       1-err 0.0% | 2-err  9.3% | 1.64 syl | 12.9
  vowel harmony         1-err 0.0% | 2-err 10.6% | 1.36 syl | 16.5
  regular derivation    1-err 6.6% | 2-err  5.3% | 1.84 syl |  2.2   <- the whole story
  all three             1-err 6.8% | 2-err  4.1% | 1.94 syl |  1.7
  RZ inherited          1-err 11.5%| 2-err  7.7% | 1.97 syl | ~0 for a zone reader

REGULAR DERIVATION cuts memorization ~8x, halves the two-error rate, costs half a syllable. Its 6.6% one-error rate is ENTIRELY collisions between morphological relatives of the same stem — the 'unrelated' column is 0.00%. A slip that turns a noun into the verb of the same root is a wrong FORM, not a wrong MEANING (RZ's instrument reports the same class separately as same-lemma). Damaging error rate stays at zero.

SWEPT THE LOAD-BEARING ASSUMPTION (how much is genuinely derivable): 2/3/4/6/8 affixes = 1000/667/500/334/250 stems. Finding survives the whole range. Even at 1000 arbitrary stems: 8.6 bits/word (half the arbitrary lexicon), zero damaging errors, two-error rate matching RZ, words still shorter than RZ's.

THE FRONTIER ANSWER: no trade-off on either axis. The structure that makes a lexicon cheap to learn is largely the SAME structure that makes it robust — a paradigm is a set of words meant to resemble each other, so their mutual confusions are cheap by construction.

RESIDUAL COST OF EZ OVER RZ, now a number: the arbitrary STEMS, 250-1000 depending on derivational productivity. Not 2000 words.

OPEN: RZ has derivation too (rz-grammar §9), so a fair head-to-head needs RZ scored on the same description-length measure — which needs a morphological analysis of RZ's lexicon that does not exist. Filed separately.

title: The humility rule protects against the wrong error: nothing screens for DROPPED segments
description:
Measured in tools/ez_mint.py, per-error-type silent rates (2000-word lexicon):

  rule                              substitution | dropped segment | inserted
  no rule (dense)                      75.8%     |     61.7%       |  21.3%
  every substitution detectable         0.0%     |     40.8%       |  11.8%
  substitutions + drops + inserts       0.0%     |      0.0%       |   0.0%
  RZ as it stands, measured            10.3%     |     17.2%       |   1.5%

A lexicon built so no two words differ by one confusable SUBSTITUTION still loses 41% of dropped-segment errors silently. GN's humility assignment rule and RZ's coinage screen are BOTH substitution-only. RZ's worst channel in the measurement is deletions (17.2%), not substitutions (10.3%) — and connected speech drops segments constantly.

This is a cheap fix and it applies to the existing lines, not just EZ: extend the screen rule from 'no unrelated minimal pairs on likely confusions' to 'no unrelated word one confusable substitution, one deletion, or one insertion away'. In a Romance-sized sound space the extension costs essentially nothing (measured: full strictness costs ~0.05 syllables/word).

Affects: GN humility rule (paper §4), RZ coinage screen (rz-lexicon.md preamble, gz-rz-mining-audit verdict 6), and the pending coinage-screen instrument.

comments.author: claude-conlang-ec
comments.text:
Numbers updated after the Codex review's denominator fix (empty percepts from deleting a one-segment word were excluded rather than counted as detected): substitution-screened lexicon 40.8% -> 38.7% of dropped-segment errors silent; RZ 17.2% -> 16.2%. The finding is unchanged and was explicitly confirmed by the reviewer as surviving the correction — substitution-only screening remains inadequate, and deletions remain RZ's worst channel (16.2% vs 10.3% for substitutions).

This bead is the most actionable result of the whole EZ round and is INDEPENDENT of every EZ-specific claim that got corrected.

title: EZ: minted lexicon kills single-segment errors, pays in tail robustness and length (claims corrected twice after review)
description:
Edward directive 2026-08-29: build the error-correction thing properly rather than auditing an inherited base. Romance-zonal phoneme space held fixed for comparability; words minted. Doc: docs/design/ez-error-corrected-lexicon.md. Instrument: tools/ez_mint.py.

HEADLINE (like-for-like, 518 words each, same confusion model, frequency-weighted):
  RZ inherited     11.5% of single slips land on a different real word | 7.7% for two slips | 1.97 syllables/word | 304 distinct syllables to learn
  EZ min-6 minted   0.0%                                              | 2.4%               | 2.00                | 134
EZ dominates on EVERY measured axis at equal word length. Alternatively at min-4: 44% shorter words (1.10 syl) with single-error immunity and roughly RZ's two-error behaviour.

So there is NO trade-off on the form axis — error correction is free or better. The entire cost is the one Edward named up front: no cognate discount.

THE DIAL: word length IS redundancy. A code built from the shortest forms is perfect against one error and fragile against two (22% silent) because two slips on a short word reach another short word — exactly the graceful-degradation failure the 2026-08-25 transcript predicted for algebraic codes. Knee is around 4 segments: half the two-error rate for 5% more length.

NOT MEASURED, and it decides everything: how much harder an arbitrary vocabulary is to learn. Next build is the structured mint (see the follow-up bead).

comments.author: claude-conlang-ec
comments.text:
CODEX REVIEW (xhigh, 2026-08-29): two BLOCKERs. The original 'dominates on every form measure / no trade-off on the form axis' claim is WITHDRAWN. Doc and paper rewritten; tools/ez_sensitivity.py added.

BLOCKER 1 — length was measured in SYLLABLES, and EZ's syllables are heavier. In segments per running word: RZ 4.36, EZ min-6 6.00 (38% LONGER, not 'equal length'), EZ min-4 4.00 (8% shorter, not 44%). No duration model exists, so neither metric alone licenses a brevity claim; both are now reported.

BLOCKER 2 — the two-error advantage is contingent on the assumed error mix. Swept (sub/drop/ins vs RZ / EZ min-4 / EZ min-6):
  60/30/10  6.8% / 8.2%  / 2.3%
  80/15/5   6.2% / 14.5% / 4.3%
  90/5/5    4.8% / 18.4% / 5.0%
  100/0/0   4.6% / 22.7% / 6.0%
Under a substitution-dominated channel RZ WINS on two errors, decisively at min-4.

WHAT SURVIVES, and it is the real result: single-segment errors stop being able to change the word. EZ 0.00% vs RZ 11.23%. Since EZ is optimized against the same confusion graph that scores it and RZ is not, the honest test is off-model — adding the e~o and i~u edges gz_redundancy itself calls attested takes EZ to 2.86% and RZ to 12.26%. A ~4x advantage survives.

THE HONEST FRAMING: EZ is excellent at the error it is designed for and degrades faster past it; RZ is mediocre everywhere and degrades gracefully. That is the textbook algebraic-vs-distributed trade, which the source transcripts predicted and which round 1 wrongly claimed to have avoided.

ALSO CORRECTED: 'length is the only fix' (false — syllable palette size changes robustness at fixed length: cap 200/400/800/1815 gives 4.9%/2.3%/3.2%/4.2% two-error); the unequal-protection causal claim about 'roominess' (untested; the 2.5-point cost is just the default mix applied to its deletion rate, 0.44 points under 90/5/5); 'like-for-like frequency weighting' (RZ empirical, EZ Zipf). Three measurement bugs fixed in ez_mint.py: two-error denominator excluded recoveries, empty-percept deletions excluded from denominators, segments/word not reported.

comments.author: claude-conlang-ec
comments.text:
ROUND 2 REVIEWED (Codex xhigh, 2026-08-29) — two BLOCKERs, both real, both fixed by rewriting tools/ez_structure.py. All round-2 numbers regenerated.

BLOCKER A — derived words were generated OUTSIDE the candidate pool, so they were never checked for phonotactic legality, distance, or harmony. Damage: 1000 of 2000 words failed legal(); 1500 derived forms sat one edit from an earlier word despite a supposedly fixed distance rule; 'all three' contained 828 illegal and 372 non-harmonic words. Example blaC -> blaCs: illegal Cs coda, counted as two syllables despite one vowel.
FIX: pack WHOLE PARADIGMS. A stem is accepted only if every word in its paradigm is legal, harmony-compatible, and >=2 errors from every word outside the paradigm; paradigm-mates may sit close, which is what a paradigm IS. Every variant now reports 0 illegal, 0 non-harmonic, 0 shortfall.

BLOCKER B — the learnability measure charged log2(surviving candidates), which depends on the size of the UNUSED pool: the same one-word lexicon cost 4 bits from a 16-form pool and 8 from a 256-form pool.
FIX: charge log2(number of legal forms of that length under the constraints in force) — a property of the phonology, not of enumeration order. Also reports an upper bound charging derived words log2(#affixes), since 'derivation is semantically transparent' is the load-bearing untestable assumption.

RESULT CHANGE: direction held, but the LENGTH COST OF DERIVATION WAS ENTIRELY HIDDEN by the bug. Corrected (2000 concepts, min 4 segments):
  arbitrary          1-err 0.00% | outside-paradigm 0.00% | 2-err 10.6% | 4.05 seg | 15.3 bits
  semantic fields          0.00% | 0.00% |  9.0% | 4.07 seg | 11.9
  vowel harmony            0.00% | 0.00% |  9.9% | 4.07 seg | 15.5
  regular derivation       6.79% | 0.00% |  5.6% | 5.17 seg |  1.9 (4.5 if opaque)
  all three                7.15% | 0.00% |  4.0% | 5.17 seg |  1.4 (4.0)
  RZ                      11.23% |   -   |  6.8% | 4.36 seg
Derivation costs 28% MORE SEGMENTS, not 'half a syllable'. The affix sweep now shows an internal trade the broken version hid: more derivation = fewer stems and better tail, but longer words.

ALSO FIXED: stale 'no trade-off' text in the tool docstring; the doc heading 'survives every assumption' (contradicted by its own 2.86% off-model figure); max(K,2) charging 1 bit for a determined form; silent concept-dropping with renormalisation; paper's 'attested confusion edges' now [D]/TODO-verify.

REFRAMED per finding 3: '0.00% outside the paradigm' means no collision crosses a generated stem group. These concepts carry NO semantics — paradigms are rank-adjacency groups — so it is NOT evidence that damaging meaning errors are zero. Real relatives can differ in polarity or reference (do/undo). Now stated as a limit, not a result.

CONFIRMED SOUND BY THE REVIEWER: all three ez_mint.py fixes from the prior round; ez_sensitivity.py has no stale-global bug and its palette and off-model sweeps are fair; the cross-stem collision arithmetic reproduces independently.

title: RZ: the polarity bit is unprotected — price the additive fix (second negation exponent)
description:
MEASURED (tools/gz_redundancy.py, docs/design/gz-progressive-redundancy.md §5): 'no'~'lo' is the worst minimal pair in RZ. 'io no vide' = I don't see it; 'io lo vide' = I see it. One preverbal clitic, one confusable substitution, opposite truth value, identical context, both perfectly grammatical. The highest-stakes bit in any utterance rides on the least protected segment in the language, and nothing checks it.

RZ CANNOT take the GZ fix: re-minting 'no' fails mining-audit gate 3 (ZERO first-contact tax, not small). So RZ needs the ADDITIVE answer — a second negation exponent realized in the high registers only, which is a rung rather than a re-mint.

Diachronic corroboration [TODO-verify at citation time]: the Jespersen cycle. French 'ne' eroded until it could not carry polarity alone and the language grew 'ne...pas'. Romance negation is EMPIRICALLY UNSTABLE as a single unstressed segment; RZ reproduced the unstable configuration from scratch.

INTERACTION WITH D1 (rz-grammar §10): D1 declares single negation equivalent to concord. With a negative indefinite present the polarity bit is duplicated and D1 is safe; in a plain positive clause 'no' is the SOLE exponent, and D1 licenses exactly the configuration that makes it unrecoverable. D1 does not need reversing — but it forecloses the obvious fix unless the second exponent is scoped to a register.

Deliverable: priced options (obligatory clause-final tag in careful/safety registers; prosodic prominence on the negator; repair-mode confirmation) + a recommendation.

comments.author: claude-conlang-ec
comments.text:
CORRECTION after Codex review (2026-08-28): the original description said D1 licenses the configuration that makes 'no' unrecoverable. That is WRONG and reverses D1's actual scope. D1 (rz-grammar §10.1) only licenses OMITTING the preverbal 'no' when a negative indefinite is present — 'io vide nada' = 'io no vide nada' — where 'nada' still carries polarity. D1 does not touch, license, or alter a plain negative clause like 'io no vide'.

Consequence: the no~lo hazard is NOT an absorption problem and no declaration change fixes it. It is a bare fact about the inventory — 'no' and 'lo' are one confusable substitution apart, both grammatical in the same preverbal slot, opposite truth value. The second negation exponent has to be specified as its own mechanism, not obtained by 'suspending D1'. D1 itself is KEEP, unchanged.

title: HUMAN GATE: does the progressive-redundancy line get its own name (PZ) or fold into GZ?
description:
Edward, 2026-08-28: 'i guess im agnostic to this living in GZ or under a new name.' Stated and left to the duke seat — this is a program question, not a technical one. Full argument: docs/design/gz-progressive-redundancy.md §12.

(a) GZ SUBSYSTEM. GZ is defined as MEDIUM channel discipline at near-Romance inventory and explicitly 'keeps most of the zonal discount'. The R2 rung spends exactly that discount, so folding it in changes what GZ IS — from 'RZ plus the channels that come cheap' to 'RZ plus the channels, including the ones that aren't'. R3/R4/R5 fit GZ's current definition without strain; R2 does not.

(b) NEW POINT ON THE DIAGRAM: **PZ — progressive zonal**. Near-Romance inventory, HIGH channel discipline, redundancy deliberately above the natural operating point, with the excess released over time. Thesis in one line: ship deliberately over-redundant and densify on evidence, because the decoder is young. Publishable on its own; paper §4.1 already states it as the general result. Cleaner story when not competing with GZ's 'cheap fruit only' framing.

(c) SPLIT BY RUNG — the recommendation. The rungs do not share a price so they should not share a home. R1/R3/R5 -> GZ now (free or transparency-POSITIVE). R4 -> GZ, register-scoped (costs hours, not transparency). R2 -> PZ or nowhere; if PZ is not worth standing up, R2 is declined with the measurement on record and both RZ and GZ live with the additive answer (second negation exponent in the high registers).

Whichever way this goes, the FINDING survives: the closed class carries ~90% of exposure to word->word corruption and 10.8% of running tokens sit one substitution from a same-slot contrast.

title: GATE: closed-class dispersion (R2) — SUPER EXPENSIVE per Edward; base-layer change, not a register; lane undecided
description:
Edward decision. gz-progressive-redundancy.md §7 measures that 80 of 96 RZ-inherited function words already clear a distance>=2 rule (no two function words, and no function word and content monosyllable, within one confusable substitution) and 16 must be re-minted: a, tu, el, si, era, la, qui, te, ala, me, elas, ha, las, lo, ni, on. Room is not the constraint — 836 mutually non-confusable monosyllabic slots remain after excluding the content lexicon's neighbourhoods (greedy lower bound) against a closed class of 96.

WHY IT MATTERS: the closed class is 15x more silent-error-prone per substitution event and 26x per unit of exposure than the content lexicon, and carries ~90% of total exposure to word->word corruption. 10.8% of running tokens are one substitution from a same-slot contrast with different truth conditions — worst pair 'no'~'lo' (negator vs object clitic, identical preverbal slot, opposite truth value).

WHY IT IS A GATE not an agent call: this visibly de-Romanizes GZ's grammar words — a capability/identity change, not an implementation detail. GZ-ONLY: RZ cannot make this purchase (mining-audit gate 3, zero first-contact tax; 'no', 'la', 'te', 'si' ARE the zonal bootstrap).

Instrument: tools/gz_redundancy.py. Doc: docs/design/gz-progressive-redundancy.md.

comments.author: claude-conlang-ec
comments.text:
REPRICED after Edward's directive (2026-08-28): 'i see this rn as *super* expensive (to zonal learning time) machinery'. The first pricing used learner-hours (~0) and was in the wrong currency — the bill is ZONAL TRANSPARENCY.

Three measured scenarios (tools/gz_redundancy.py):
  S1 strict distance>=2, no exemptions -> 16 re-mints = 5.4% of running tokens made non-Romance. This is the version Edward priced, and he is right.
  S2 + Tier-3 near-synonyms licensed (le~la, les~las, que~qui, eles~elas — the starboard/larboard rule's own escape clause) -> 12 re-mints = 4.8%.
  S3 + DONOR-VARIANT RE-SELECTION -> 8 re-mints = 1.8%. The cheap door: for several hazard forms the zone offers a second attested variant that already clears the rule, so dispersion is bought by re-picking inside the donor space rather than coining. no->non (IT/FR non — fixes the worst pair in the language, no~lo, at NEGATIVE zonal cost), a->ad, tu->tuo, te->ti, dos->due, tras->detras.
  Residue after S3: el, si, era, ala, me, ha, ni, on — and that is an upper bound (ha->habe; 'on' deletable in favour of the impersonal reflexive RZ already has; 'ala' is already flagged coined-ish).

STRUCTURAL ARGUMENT AGAINST FOLDING IT INTO GZ: R2 is the only rung of the ladder that is not a register — it is a permanent lexical property, so it is the ONLY rung that cannot be dialled back as the community matures. A ladder whose expensive rung is the irreversible one is badly shaped.

BLOCKED ON: the lane decision (see the PZ bead). Recommendation in gz-progressive-redundancy.md §12(c): R1/R3/R4/R5 -> GZ; R2 -> a new PZ line or declined outright with the measurement on record. Do NOT smuggle R2 into GZ.

comments.author: claude-conlang-ec
comments.text:
NUMBERS CORRECTED (same day). The first dispersion run enforced only half the stated rule — function words were checked against each other but NOT against the content lexicon, though the rule reads 'no two function words, AND no function word and content monosyllable, within one confusable substitution'. Fixed in tools/gz_redundancy.py. Corrected scenarios:

  S1 strict            -> 24 of 96 re-mints = 7.6% of running tokens made non-Romance (was 16 / 5.4%)
  S2 + Tier-3 licensed -> 20 of 96 = 7.0%
  S3 + re-selection    -> 15 of 96 = 4.0% (was 8 / 1.8%)
  S3 residue: el, quando, tote, nos, si, era, sin, ala, cata, me, ante, ha, ni, on, ora

The correction makes the purchase MORE expensive, i.e. it strengthens Edward's read rather than weakening it. The no->non re-selection still fixes the worst pair in the language at zero or negative zonal cost.

Two reasons 4.0% remains an UPPER bound: (a) more donor doors exist (ha->habe; 'on' deletable in favour of the impersonal reflexive; 'ala' already coined-ish; 'ora' collides with 'hora' only because h is silent); (b) the optimization is ONE-SIDED — it holds the content lexicon fixed and always moves the function word. Eight of the fifteen are function-vs-content collisions (tote~pote, nos~dos, sin~fin, ante~alte, cata~casa, quando~quanto, ora~hora) where the CONTENT word is rarer and cheaper to move. A joint optimization would land materially lower. Not run: 'which side moves' is a taste call, not a number.

comments.author: claude-conlang-ec
comments.text:
CODEX REVIEW (xhigh, 2026-08-28) landed; two BLOCKERs, both fixed, and one changes what R2 IS.

BLOCKER A — R2 is not a rung. It substitutes forms rather than adding signal, so it fails the ladder's own monotonicity test: a lower-rung reader cannot strip it. title: Redesign cloze-test-v0 to LOCATE the usability threshold, not just report a headline number
description:
The instrument is currently built to answer "what percent do readers comprehend?" The question that actually decides RZ's design is "AT WHAT COMPREHENSION LEVEL DOES TEXT BECOME USABLE?" — a different measurement, and the repo has no plan to make it.

## Why this is the load-bearing task in the epic

Everything in conlang-ym3 reduces to the shape of the comprehension-to-usefulness curve. If usability is a step around 85-90%, concentrating on the Ibero bloc dominates and Edward's population instinct is right. If it is linear, the centroid wins. Nobody in the project knows which, and it is cheap to find out relative to what it decides.

## What has to change

1. **Add a usability outcome alongside the cloze score.** Cloze percentage is the predictor; the dependent variable needs to be something like "did you finish the passage," "can you answer comprehension questions about it," "would you keep reading," or task success on the content. Without a second axis there is no curve to find a knee in.
2. **Span the range deliberately.** The current design tests RZ text at whatever comprehension it happens to produce. To locate a threshold you need passages spanning roughly 60-95% comprehension per reader — which means constructing or selecting graded variants, not just measuring one corpus.
3. **Report per-source-language distributions, not just the mean.** Under objective C (ym3.2) the quantity of interest is "how many readers clear the bar," which a mean actively hides. An 84%-style headline is compatible with everyone at 84% or with half at 95% and half at 73%, and those two worlds call for opposite designs.
4. **Reconcile with the published benchmark.** Interslavic's 84% is an unweighted cross-language mean. If RZ reports something else, say plainly why — the comparison is the pitch (romance-zonal-v0.md §7.1) and changing the metric without flagging it reads as gaming.

## Constraint

Edward 2026-08-15: NO cloze/human testing yet. This bead is instrument DESIGN only — the protocol, the graded passages, the analysis plan — held until human testing is authorized. Design it now so the first real run answers the question that matters instead of the question that was easy to ask.

Depends on ym3.2 for which objective the instrument serves, though most of the redesign is robust across A/B/C.

title: DECISION: what does RZ maximize — population above a usability threshold, or mean comprehension?
description:
HUMAN GATE. This is the one-way door under the whole weighting question, and it changes what RZ ends up being — not merely how it is built.

## The three candidate objectives

**A. Maximize population-weighted mean comprehension.** Weight sources by reader base; accept that ES+PT (.82 of the zone) decide nearly everything. Product: "regularized Spanish with Portuguese and Italian loans." Highest raw reach, reads as Spanish hegemony to the IT/FR/RO communities.

**B. Maximize unweighted mean across sources (the centroid).** Interlingua's and Interslavic's implicit choice. Everyone lands ~75%; nobody lands at 95%. Neutral-looking, and matches the metric RZ already plans to publish.

**C. Maximize population ABOVE A USABILITY THRESHOLD.** Recommended by the analysis. Treats comprehension as step-shaped rather than linear: 95% lets you read a novel, 70% makes you bounce off paragraph one. Under this objective, whether to concentrate or spread is an EMPIRICAL question, not a taste question.

## Why C is the recommendation

It is the only one of the three that does not smuggle in an untested assumption. A and B each presuppose the shape of the comprehension-to-usefulness curve; C makes that shape the thing you measure (conlang-ym3.3) and then derives the weights from the answer.

If the threshold turns out to sit around 85-90%, C reproduces A's concentration and Edward's naive population instinct is vindicated. If comprehension is roughly linear in usefulness, C reproduces B. Either way the weights stop being taste.

## The strongest argument against neutrality, stated fairly

Interslavic has an admirable measured 84% and a few thousand speakers. Neutrality has not actually produced adoption anywhere in auxlang history. If comprehension is threshold-shaped, B optimizes a number that corresponds to no usable product for anyone.

## The strongest argument against concentration, stated fairly

Adoption incentive runs OPPOSITE to population. A Spanish speaker already has ~500M interlocutors and near-zero reason to adopt an auxlang; a Romanian has 24M and a real one. Interlingua's community concentrated in SCANDINAVIA, not in any source-language homeland (zonal-auxlang-survey.md §1.1). Under A, RZ maximizes reach to precisely the cohort least motivated to adopt, while looking like Spanish imperialism to the cohort that supplies adopters.

## What Edward needs to decide

Not the weights. Only: **is RZ a reach product or a neutrality product, and are we willing to let a measurement settle it?** Choosing C is choosing to let the cloze data decide, which is the deferral-friendly option and the one the agent recommends.

Blocks: the §1 weight scheme, the §4 tie-break reconciliation, the ym3.4 re-derivation, and (largely) conlang-wan.
close_reason: ADOPTED option C provisionally (agent-called 2026-08-30 under the landing directive; the deferral-friendly option — commits to nothing except letting the cloze data decide the weights; Edward may override): RZ maximizes zone readers ABOVE A USABILITY THRESHOLD, not mean comprehension. Recorded in romance-zonal-v0.md §1 and paper §11. With RZ an Interlingua profile (wan), concentrate-vs-centroid IS the profile-vs-baseline measurement. Unblocks 8zy and ym3.4; ym3.3 feeds the pilot 5i1.1. Dep on ym3.1 (verify population figures) does not gate the objective choice — force-closed.

title: EPIC: own the RZ objective function (weights, tie-breaks, and the cloze instrument optimize unstated targets)
description:
THE LEVEL-UP. Edward 2026-08-28 asked whether to weight RZ source languages by speaker population. "Which weights" has no answer until RZ states what it is maximizing — and it never has. Edward's call: own this, but DEFER it (filed 2026-08-28, not started).

## The problem

Three artifacts currently optimize three unstated and possibly different targets:

1. **romance-zonal-v0.md §1 source weights** (ES .40, PT .25, IT .15, FR .15, RO .05). Described as "reader-base share of the zone." They are not — approx L1 shares are ES .55, PT .27, FR .08, IT .07, RO .03. The numbers are actually an unlabeled hedge between two real schemes: population weighting (Ibero bloc .82) and Interlingua's control-group rule (Ibero .25, ES/PT deliberately collapsed to one vote of four).

2. **romance-zonal-v0.md §4 lexicon tie-breaks** (weighted sight-recognition -> derivation-family regularity -> English/international cognate -> shorter). This is a lexicographic ordering, not a weighted objective, and it has never been reconciled with §1's weights. Two different aggregation rules for the same decision.

3. **cloze-test-v0.md** — built to produce a headline mean benchmarked against Interslavic's 84%. That 84% is an UNWEIGHTED cross-language mean, from a language that balances across Slavic branches rather than weighting toward Russian. If the design population-weights while the metric means, design and scoreboard disagree by construction.

## The question that decides it

Is comprehension threshold-shaped or linear? At ~95% you read a novel; at ~70% you bounce off paragraph one. If usability is a step around 85-90%, CONCENTRATING dominates — 720M ES+PT readers above threshold beats 900M readers all sitting just below. If comprehension is linear in usefulness, the centroid wins and neutrality is correct.

Nothing in the repo measures this. It decides the entire weighting argument, and it is empirically answerable with the cloze instrument already planned.

## Scope of ownership

State the objective function in romance-zonal-v0.md as a first-class design commitment, then make §1 weights, §4 tie-breaks, and the cloze instrument all DERIVE from it rather than each carrying its own implicit target. Re-derive every flagged decision under the result.

## Downstream

conlang-wan (RZ-as-Interlingua-profile vs fourth fork) largely resolves from this: population weighting is the single change that most differentiates RZ from Interlingua, since it flips querer/poder, entonce, ventana, and lunes/martes all Ibero.

## Analysis already done

Full argument (double-counting the Ibero bloc, asymmetric recognition, adoption incentive running opposite to population, metric mismatch, and the threshold steelman) is in conlang-8zy. Population figures throughout are from memory and are themselves a child task to verify.

title: RZ source weights: state the objective function, fix the misdescription, collapse the Ibero bloc
description:
Edward 2026-08-28 asked whether to weight source languages by speaker population.

FINDING 1 (doc bug, fixable now): romance-zonal-v0.md section 1 says 'Weights approx reader-base share of the zone.' They are not. Approx L1 shares: ES .55, PT .27, FR .08, IT .07, RO .03. RZ uses ES .40, PT .25, IT .15, FR .15, RO .05 — a real judgment (downweight ES, upweight IT/FR) presented as arithmetic. Either restate the basis or change the numbers.

FINDING 2 (three schemes, RZ sits silently between two): population-weighted gives Ibero bloc .82; RZ today .65; Interlingua .25 (ES/PT deliberately collapsed to ONE control group of four).

CONSEQUENCE of pure population weighting: every section 9 open question resolves Ibero — querer/poder over voler/poter, entonce over alora, ventana over fenestra, lunes/martes over lunedi/martedi. RZ becomes 'regularized Spanish', which incidentally RESOLVES conlang-wan toward fork (it is the single change that most differentiates RZ from Interlingua).

ARGUMENTS AGAINST pure population: (a) ES+PT agree on most contested items, so counting them separately double-counts one decision — Interlingua's bloc collapse is the precedented fix and the piece RZ lacks; (b) recognition is asymmetric — ES readers recover Italo-Latin forms via derivation families, IT/RO readers cannot recover janela/ventana from anything, so the scarce resource is recognition by small groups; (c) adoption incentive runs opposite to population (Interlingua's community concentrated in Scandinavia, not any source homeland); (d) METRIC MISMATCH — the pitch benchmarks Interslavic's 84%, an UNWEIGHTED mean across sources from a language that balances across Slavic branches rather than weighting toward Russian. Population-weighting the design while publishing a mean optimizes one thing and scores another.

STEELMAN FOR population weighting (strong): comprehension is probably threshold-shaped, not linear. At 95% you read a novel, at 70% you bounce. If the usability threshold is 85-90%, concentrating beats spreading — 720M ES+PT above threshold beats 900M all just below it. Interslavic has 84% and a few thousand speakers.

RECOMMENDATION: (1) collapse ES+PT into one bloc where they agree — highest value, independent of everything else; (2) state the objective as maximize population ABOVE A COMPREHENSION THRESHOLD, not maximize the mean, and make the published metric match; (3) design cloze-test-v0 to LOCATE the threshold, not just report a headline number. Ibero-collapsed population weighting lands near ES+PT .55 / FR .20 / IT .18 / RO .07, close to today's numbers — so current weights are roughly defensible but undocumented.

Population figures are from memory; verify before acting. Objective-function choice is a human gate; the doc-bug fix and the cloze-test redesign are not.

title: Price RZ-as-Interlingua-profile vs RZ-as-fourth-fork
description:
Systematic comparison: RZ is ~80-85% Interlingua at the grammar level. Literally shared, not merely similar: le/un articles, -e adjectives (calde/forte/prime/nove/tote/multe/iste/mesme/nostre), -te participles, person-invariant verbs + obligatory subject pronouns, no gender/case/subjunctive, plus / le plus, the entire -itate/-mente/-al/-or/-ista/-ia/-bile/re-/des-/in- derivation family, io/tu/nos/vos, es/era/va, -va past, near-identical weekdays and months.

Real deltas: shallow orthography (-cion vs -tion, no Greek digraphs, no double consonants); Ibero weighting (dos/cuatro/cinco/ses/sete/nove; en/por/sobre/necun/aquel/altre vs IA in/pro/super/nulle/celle/altere); negative concord; es-vs-sta; adjective number agreement + les; analytic future va+inf and -ria conditional vs IA synthetic -ra/-rea; tener-perfect and sta-progressive. Plus three layers IA lacks entirely: the closed 96-form function-word guarantee, the variation-absorption declarations, and the measurement+tooling program.

Implication: RZ differentiators are governance/measurement/tooling, not language design. Interlingua is frozen since IALA closed 1953 and UMI is promotional not regulatory - but it has a 27k-word dictionary, a Wikipedia edition, and decades of periodicals. romance-zonal-v0.md section 7.5 warns against the Interlingua/Neolatino/LFN fork pathology, and RZ as currently specced IS a fourth fork.

Decide before further RZ lexicon spend: ship RZ as a declared *Interlingua profile* (shallow-orthography Ibero variant, inherits the corpus) vs a clean-break fork. Positioning / one-way-door call -> human gate.

title: Reorder the linear stream instead of leaving it: instruction-scheduling for prose (Edward's CPU idea)
description:
Edward 2026-08-27: 'we might take inspo from CPU rearrangement of machine code. CPUs are optimized for single-threaded processing.'

WHY THIS IS BETTER THAN WHAT THE SPATIAL LANE HAS BEEN DOING. An out-of-order CPU takes a LINEAR instruction stream, reconstructs its dependency graph internally (register renaming kills false dependencies), issues work as operands become ready, and retires IN ORDER so the observable semantics are untouched. The programmer never writes a graph. The graph is recovered, exploited, and hidden.

Map that onto reading and the analogy inverts our whole approach. The READER is the serial machine — 39 bits/s, serial binding, one relation at a time (Franconeri). So the move is not 'hand the reader a graph'; it is 'REORDER THE LINEAR STREAM SO THE SERIAL MACHINE STALLS LESS'. Same notation, same prose, zero new symbols, ZERO LEARNING COST — which matters enormously given how much of the spatial lane's problem is acquisition cost.

CONCRETE MECHANISMS, each with a direct compiler analogue:
- REGISTER PRESSURE / LIVE RANGES. We already measure a 'serial binding span': mean 7.1 intervening tokens between successive mentions of a referent, worst 16. That IS register pressure. A compiler schedules to shorten live ranges; we can reorder clauses to shorten the distance between a referent's mentions. Same content, same linear format, less to hold.
- HOISTING / PREFETCH. Introduce a referent before the clause that needs it, the way a compiler hoists a load above a branch.
- BRANCH PREDICTION. Put the predictable continuation on the fall-through path; mark the unexpected one (UNLWS already has an 'unexpectedly' line decoration).
- IN-ORDER RETIREMENT is the constraint, and it is the important one: whatever we reorder in PRESENTATION, the reader's final model must be identical. Reordering must preserve entailments, scope, and temporal facts — which is exactly the oracle-coverage gate we already built.

EXISTING PRIOR ART, and it is strong: CENTERING THEORY (Grosz, Joshi and Weinstein) is the linguistics version of this — it ranks transitions between sentences (CONTINUE > RETAIN > SMOOTH-SHIFT > ROUGH-SHIFT) by how much referent-tracking cost they impose, and there is a real literature on entity-based coherence and on sentence ordering in NLG. So the idea is not speculative; it has been studied under another name, and nobody appears to have applied it as a DESIGNED FEATURE of a constructed language.

WHY IT SUITS THIS PROJECT SPECIFICALLY: GZ's parse is deterministic, so we can compute the dependency graph exactly rather than approximating it — the same property that made the spatial layer possible, applied to a cheaper output. And an optimizing 'text scheduler' is a tool that works on ORDINARY GZ PROSE, so it needs no reader buy-in at all.

FIRST EXPERIMENT (cheap, uses the existing harness): implement a clause scheduler that reorders a discourse to minimize total binding span subject to preserving the oracle fields, measure the span reduction, and run the train/test protocol on scheduled vs unscheduled prose. Prediction to falsify: scheduled prose beats unscheduled on referent-tracking questions with no notation change and no training.

title: Spatial layer: test NON-NARRATIVE content (the untested case that probably matters most)
description: Every specimen built so far is narrative. Edward 2026-08-27: 'time tends to be linear but it's not always there or there enough to be linear.' Definitions, taxonomies, specifications, arguments and procedures have little or no temporal sequence — which is exactly the content where a linear control is WEAKEST (prose has to serialize a structure that is not inherently ordered) and where a spatial layer should be strongest. It is also where the Codex direction review located the killer application: contracts, procedural texts, semantic diffing, translation checking. Concretely: extend tools/spatial_layer.py with non-narrative source types — a taxonomy (X is a kind of Y, with cross-cutting properties), a specification (conditions and exceptions), and an argument (claims, evidence, objections) — and run the existing train/test protocol on them against the same linear control. Prediction to falsify: the spatial layouts' disadvantage shrinks or reverses on non-narrative content, because clause ORDER stops being information the layout has to preserve. Note this also relaxes S3-style failures: a ring layout loses clause order, which is fatal for narrative and free for a taxonomy.

A writing system that spends learning time to buy something is something I'm willing to entertain.' Each subsystem may SPEND learner hours if it BUYS something worth the hours — the same purchase-ledger logic learning-budget.md already applies. Every mechanism gets priced, not vetoed.

Every layout we have built assumes the opposite asymmetry and spends ink encoding it. Either the asymmetry is real and UNLWS pays for symmetry with reading-order ambiguity, or it is an artefact of the languages we know and our layouts are wasting ink. Testable with the train/test harness, and worth testing BEFORE committing to place structure, since declared places bake the asymmetry in.

title: Read UNLWS (Unker Non-Linear Writing System) before designing further spatial rounds
description: Prior-art survey 2026-08-26 found the closest existing prior art: UNLWS by Sai and Alex Fink (s.ai/nlws; design essay s.ai/essays/nlf2dws). It is essentially this project, built by serious conlangers: glyphs are predicates whose ATTACHMENT POINTS are symbolically related to their argument roles; texts are assembled by joining glyphs so shared attachment points mean shared referents; no inherent reading order; oligosynthetic lexicon; connection types for copular relations, causation, evidentiality, and remote coreference. Sai's own list of difficulties maps onto our open problems exactly: sequential events force linear connections inside a non-linear system; it does not fit a book and 'chopped up into 8.5x11 chunks' damages comprehension; insertion/deletion are hard; layout must be planned ahead (premature commitment); 'difficult for people who think linearly / verbally'. His comprehension claims are cautious and unevidenced. Action: read the essay and the Prayer of St Francis specimen, extract the mechanisms worth stealing (attachment-point role encoding especially), and record what UNLWS already settles so we do not re-walk it.

title: Greedy repair's ordering is right and its stopping rule is wrong
description:
Round 5: greedy-by-damage dominates random at MATCHED repair count (65 repairs: 1.12% vs 1.75% off-model, 76.4% vs 74.5% of running text kept). But greedy STOPS when no in-model hazard remains, at 71 repairs and 1.12% off-model, while random continues to 87 (0.44%) and rarest-first to 92 (0.23%). Repairs keep buying off-model robustness after the in-model rate has already hit zero.

Consequence for policy: migrating an existing language under a change budget wants greedy ordering with an early stop; DESIGNING a lexicon wants greedy ordering and no stop, because repair count is a one-time design cost and the final lexicon is what speakers live with. Repairing against the wider graph is the same lesson stated forward — 8 points of strict transparency for 1.12% -> 0.16% off-model.

Open: the continuation rule past the in-model hazard set is unspecified. Needs a slack measure to order by.

title: Paper §2 + brief overstate Coupé et al.: ~39 bit/s is a mean over read speech, not a proven universal ceiling
description:
Found by the Codex review of the Ithkuil steal-pass (2026-08-30), which checked the primary source. The finding applies to the new doc AND to pre-existing project text, which is why this is filed separately — the new doc has been corrected already (docs/design/alternatives/ithkuil-forks.md §2).

WHAT THE SOURCE SAYS: Coupé, Oh, Dediu & Pellegrino (2019, Sci. Adv.) measured READ speech in 17 natural languages and found information rate clustering near a MEAN of 39.15 bit/s, with real variation across languages and speakers.

WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH: (a) a universal cognitive ceiling; (b) a causal one-for-one density/rate compensation mechanism; (c) anything about spontaneous conversation; (d) anything about constructed languages, whose speakers are all L2 learners composing deliberately. Its information-theoretic measure is also not the same object as 'explicitly marked semantic distinctions'.

WHERE THE OVERCLAIM SITS:
- paper/paper.md §1: 'empirically pinned by cognition, not by the code'
- paper/paper.md §2: 'The ceiling appears to be cognitive rather than articulatory' — 'appears' is doing a lot of work; the surrounding text treats it as settled
- docs/design-brief.md, Goal/non-goals: 'pinned by cognition regardless of code'
- README.md 'approximately zero gains in how fast a human can talk'

WHY IT MATTERS: this premise is load-bearing — it is the stated reason speech throughput is a project NON-GOAL, and the reason the wide-phonology branch is dead. The non-goal decision survives the weaker reading fine (weak evidence for 'don't optimize this' is still a reason not to optimize it). What does not survive is the paper stating it as established fact, which violates the project's own evidence discipline.

DELIVERABLE: reword §1/§2/brief/README to the defensible version — a robust cross-linguistic regularity in a controlled reading task, which makes large throughput gains unlikely [H] rather than impossible. Keep the non-goal. Check @rayner2016/@irest2012/@brysbaert2019 in the same pass for the same failure mode (the reading-rate convergence claim is stated equally strongly).

3. THE EXPONENT IS THE HARD PART and was hand-waved as 'open'. It is blocking: the coda is already spent on POS (SPEC §6); an extra syllable changes the word's phonological shape (so it is not obviously different from ordinary compounding/derivation); and a script-only marker leaves spoken forms homophonous, which breaks the four-projections determinism the spec relies on.

4. Learning cost must be priced as TWO line items — the productive rule (small) and the per-cell vocabulary (not small) — not one.
